config.title: Generic useFetch<T>

intro.title: Generic useFetch<T>
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a reusable custom React hook called `useFetch<T>` that fetches data from an API. You will learn how to use TypeScript generics to make the hook flexible and type-safe, allowing it to return data of any specified type. The main technologies involved are React hooks (like `useState` and `useEffect`), TypeScript generics, and asynchronous JavaScript with `fetch`. By the end, you'll have a hook that handles loading and error states while providing strongly-typed data for your components.
intro.usecase: Generic useFetch<T> is essential in data-driven React applications where you need to fetch different types of data with consistent loading, error, and success states. In e-commerce dashboards, you'd use it to fetch product listings, user orders, and inventory data—each with different TypeScript interfaces but the same fetching logic. Admin panels use this pattern to load user profiles, analytics metrics, and audit logs while maintaining type safety across all API responses. This approach eliminates code duplication when building complex interfaces like data tables with filters, real-time notification feeds, or multi-step forms that fetch configuration data.

objectives: Implement a generic TypeScript interface for API response data
Construct a custom React hook with generic type parameters
Initialize state variables to manage loading, error, and data states
Manipulate the hook's internal logic to handle different data types
Apply the generic useFetch hook to fetch user data from an API
Integrate the hook's return values into component rendering logic
Configure the hook to accept different endpoint URLs dynamically

steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and the two hooks we'll need for state and side effects.

steps.title: Initialize state variables for data, loading, and error
steps.instruction: Inside your useFetch function, use useState to create three state variables: data (initialized to null), loading (initialized to true), and error (initialized to null).
steps.hint: Call useState three times, each with its initial value. Remember to destructure the array to get the state variable and setter function for each.
steps.expectedOutcome: Your useFetch function will have three state variables ready to track the fetched data, loading status, and any errors.
successCriteria: The useFetch function contains three useState calls that initialize data to null, loading to true, and error to null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created some state variables, but make sure you have all three: data, loading, and error with their correct initial values.
steps.feedbackWrong: The state variables aren't set up correctly. You need three useState calls inside useFetch with the specified initial values.

steps.title: Define the fetchData async helper function
steps.instruction: Inside the useFetch function, define an async function named fetchData that will handle the fetch request.
steps.hint: Write 'async function fetchData() { }' or 'const fetchData = async () => { }' inside the useFetch function body.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useFetch function now contains an empty async fetchData helper function.
successCriteria: An async function named fetchData is defined inside the useFetch function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've defined an async function named fetchData inside the useFetch function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The fetchData async helper function is not properly defined inside useFetch.

steps.title: Add useEffect to call fetchData when URL changes
steps.instruction: Inside the useFetch hook, add a useEffect hook that calls fetchData when the url parameter changes. Include url in the dependency array and add a cleanup function to abort the fetch if the component unmounts.
steps.hint: Call useEffect with an arrow function that invokes fetchData. Return a cleanup function that sets an abort flag or uses AbortController if you plan to implement it later.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useEffect hook is added, calling fetchData when url changes, with proper dependency array and cleanup function.
successCriteria: useEffect is called with fetchData inside, url is in the dependency array, and a cleanup function is returned.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to include url in the dependency array and add a cleanup function.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the syntax: useEffect should be called with an arrow function that calls fetchData, include [url] as dependency, and return a cleanup function.

steps.title: Return the state values from the useFetch hook
steps.instruction: At the end of your useFetch hook, return an object containing the data, loading, and error state values.
steps.hint: Make the hook's state available to components that use it by returning these values.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useFetch hook now returns an object with data, loading, and error properties, making these values accessible to any component that calls the hook.
successCriteria: The useFetch hook returns an object containing data, loading, and error.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're returning an object with exactly three properties: data, loading, and error.
steps.feedbackWrong: The hook needs to return an object containing the data, loading, and error state values. Check that you're returning these three values from the hook.

steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns a JSX wrapper element (like a div).
steps.hint: Define a function called App that returns a div element. This will be the main component that uses the useFetch hook.
steps.expectedOutcome: A functional component named App is defined, returning a JSX wrapper element.
successCriteria: The App component is defined as a function (or arrow function) and returns a JSX element (e.g., a div).

steps.title: Use the useFetch hook in App with a sample API URL
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, call the useFetch hook with the URL 'https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1' and destructure the returned object into variables named data, loading, and error.
steps.hint: Call the hook at the top of your component function and destructure its return value. The hook returns an object with data, loading, and error properties.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component will have access to the data, loading, and error states from the useFetch hook when called with the sample URL.
successCriteria: The useFetch hook is called with the sample URL inside App, and its return value is destructured into data, loading, and error variables.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Add conditional rendering for loading state
steps.instruction: In your App component's JSX, add a conditional check that returns a paragraph with the text 'Loading...' when the loading state is true.
steps.hint: Use a logical AND (&&) operator or a ternary to conditionally render the loading message based on the loading variable.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component will display a 'Loading...' message when data is being fetched.
successCriteria: The App component's JSX includes a conditional that renders a paragraph with 'Loading...' text when loading is true.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the loading message only appears when loading is true.
steps.feedbackWrong: The loading message isn't appearing conditionally. Check your conditional logic and ensure it uses the loading variable.

steps.title: Display the fetched data when available
steps.instruction: In your App component's JSX, add a section that displays the fetched data when loading is false and error is null. You can use a <pre> tag to show the data in a readable format.
steps.hint: Add a condition after the error check to render the data. Use the destructured data variable from the useFetch hook.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component will now display the fetched JSON data in a formatted way when the request is successful.
successCriteria: The App component includes a condition that renders the data (e.g., inside a <pre> tag) when loading is false and error is null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're conditionally rendering the data only when loading is false and error is null.
steps.feedbackWrong: The data display isn't working as expected. Check that you're using the correct condition and rendering the data variable.
